problems.title: High earners
problems.statement: Show `emp_name` and `salary` of employees earning **more than 50,000**, highest salary first.
problems.solution: SELECT emp_name, salary FROM emp WHERE salary > 50000 ORDER BY salary DESC;
problems.hint: `WHERE` filters rows; `ORDER BY ... DESC` sorts descending.

problems.title: Employees without a department
problems.statement: List the names of employees who have **no department** (`dept_id` is missing).
problems.solution: SELECT emp_name FROM emp WHERE dept_id IS NULL;
problems.hint: `= NULL` is never true. Which operator tests for NULL?
problems.explain: Comparisons with NULL are UNKNOWN, so `dept_id = NULL` returns no rows. Use `IS NULL`.

problems.title: Names starting with a letter
problems.statement: Show the names of employees whose name **starts with `A`, `B` or `C`**, in alphabetical order.
problems.solution: SELECT emp_name FROM emp WHERE emp_name LIKE 'A%' OR emp_name LIKE 'B%' OR emp_name LIKE 'C%' ORDER BY emp_name;
problems.oracle: SELECT emp_name FROM emp WHERE REGEXP_LIKE(emp_name, '^[ABC]') ORDER BY emp_name;
problems.hint: `%` matches any run of characters. Oracle has no `[ABC]` wildcard in LIKE.

problems.title: Salary bands
problems.statement: For each employee show `emp_name` and a `band`: `'High'` if salary >= 60000, `'Mid'` if >= 40000, otherwise `'Low'`. Order by `emp_id`.
problems.solution: SELECT emp_name, CASE WHEN salary >= 60000 THEN 'High' WHEN salary >= 40000 THEN 'Mid' ELSE 'Low' END AS band FROM emp ORDER BY emp_id;
problems.hint: `CASE WHEN ... THEN ... WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END`. Conditions are checked top to bottom.

problems.title: Top 3 salaries
problems.statement: Show the **three highest-paid** employees (`emp_name`, `salary`), highest first.
problems.solution: SELECT emp_name, salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 3;
problems.oracle: SELECT emp_name, salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY;
problems.note: SQLite uses `LIMIT`. In Oracle 12c+ write `FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY` (older: `ROWNUM` on a sorted subquery).

problems.title: Total compensation
problems.statement: Show `emp_name` and `total` = salary + commission for employees in department **30**, treating a missing commission as 0. Order by `emp_name`.
problems.solution: SELECT emp_name, salary + COALESCE(comm, 0) AS total FROM emp WHERE dept_id = 30 ORDER BY emp_name;
problems.oracle: SELECT emp_name, salary + NVL(comm, 0) AS total FROM emp WHERE dept_id = 30 ORDER BY emp_name;
problems.hint: `salary + NULL` is NULL. Replace NULL with a default first.

problems.title: Average salary per department
problems.statement: For each department (by **name**) show the average salary as `avg_sal`, rounded to a whole number. Only departments that have employees. Order by department name.
problems.solution: SELECT d.dept_name, ROUND(AVG(e.salary)) AS avg_sal FROM emp e JOIN dept d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_name ORDER BY d.dept_name;
problems.hint: Join to get the name, then `GROUP BY` it. Every non-aggregated column must be grouped.

problems.title: Departments with more than 2 people
problems.statement: List `dept_id` and the number of employees (`cnt`) for departments with **more than 2 employees**. Ignore employees without a department.
problems.solution: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM emp WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 2 ORDER BY dept_id;
problems.hint: `WHERE` filters rows *before* grouping; `HAVING` filters groups *after*.

problems.title: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)
problems.statement: In one row show `total_emp` (all employees) and `with_comm` (employees who **have** a commission).
problems.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_emp, COUNT(comm) AS with_comm FROM emp;

problems.title: Departments with no employees (NOT IN trap)
problems.statement: List the names of departments that have **no employees**. Careful: one employee has a NULL department, so the obvious `NOT IN (SELECT dept_id FROM emp)` returns **nothing**. Write it so it works.
problems.solution: SELECT dept_name FROM dept d WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM emp e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id);
problems.hint: `NOT IN` with a NULL in the list is UNKNOWN for every row. `NOT EXISTS` (or `LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL`) is NULL-safe.
problems.explain: A NULL in the subquery makes `x NOT IN (...)` UNKNOWN for every x. Use `NOT EXISTS` or a `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL`.

problems.title: Employees with their department
problems.statement: Show `emp_name` and `dept_name` for every employee that **has** a department. Order by `emp_id`.
problems.solution: SELECT e.emp_name, d.dept_name FROM emp e JOIN dept d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id ORDER BY e.emp_id;
problems.oracle:
SELECT e.emp_name, d.dept_name FROM emp e JOIN dept d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id ORDER BY e.emp_id;
-- note: no AS before a table alias in Oracle

problems.title: Keep employees without a department
problems.statement: Show **every** employee with their `dept_name` (NULL if none). Order by `emp_id`.
problems.solution: SELECT e.emp_name, d.dept_name FROM emp e LEFT JOIN dept d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id ORDER BY e.emp_id;
problems.hint: Which side must keep all its rows?

problems.title: Employee and manager
problems.statement: Show each employee's name and their manager's name (`manager`). The CEO has no manager: show NULL. Order by employee `emp_id`.
problems.solution: SELECT e.emp_name, m.emp_name AS manager FROM emp e LEFT JOIN emp m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id ORDER BY e.emp_id;
problems.hint: Join the table to itself with two aliases. LEFT join keeps the CEO.

problems.title: Everyone and every department
problems.statement: List all pairs of `emp_name` and `dept_name`, **including** employees without a department and departments without employees. Order by `dept_name`, then `emp_name` (NULLs last).
problems.solution: SELECT e.emp_name, d.dept_name FROM emp e FULL JOIN dept d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id ORDER BY d.dept_name IS NULL, d.dept_name, e.emp_name IS NULL, e.emp_name;
problems.oracle:
SELECT e.emp_name, d.dept_name FROM emp e FULL OUTER JOIN dept d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id ORDER BY d.dept_name, e.emp_name;
-- Oracle sorts NULLs last in ASC order by default
problems.hint: Which join keeps unmatched rows from both sides?

problems.title: Earning more than the manager
problems.statement: Find employees who earn **more than their manager**. Show `emp_name`, `salary` and the manager's `mgr_salary`. (There may be none — that is a valid answer.)
problems.solution: SELECT e.emp_name, e.salary, m.salary AS mgr_salary FROM emp e JOIN emp m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id WHERE e.salary > m.salary;
problems.hint: Two aliases of the same table; compare the salaries in `WHERE`.

problems.title: Pairs with the same salary
problems.statement: List pairs of employees with the **same salary**: `emp_1`, `emp_2`, `salary`, each pair once, ordered by salary descending.
problems.solution: SELECT a.emp_name AS emp_1, b.emp_name AS emp_2, a.salary FROM emp a JOIN emp b ON a.salary = b.salary AND a.emp_id < b.emp_id ORDER BY a.salary DESC;
problems.hint: `a.emp_id < b.emp_id` removes self-pairs and mirrored duplicates.

problems.title: Cities with both customers and suppliers
problems.statement: Show the cities that have **both** a customer and a supplier (`city`), alphabetically.
problems.solution: SELECT city FROM customers INTERSECT SELECT city FROM suppliers ORDER BY city;
problems.hint: Which set operator keeps only rows found in both queries?

problems.title: Above the company average
problems.statement: List the names of employees earning **more than the average salary** of the whole company. Order by name.
problems.solution: SELECT emp_name FROM emp WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp) ORDER BY emp_name;
problems.hint: The subquery returns a single value.

problems.title: Second highest salary
problems.statement: Return the **second highest distinct salary** as `second_highest`.
problems.solution: SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp);
problems.hint: The highest value among those smaller than the maximum.

problems.title: Above their department's average
problems.statement: List employees who earn **more than the average of their own department**. Show `emp_name`. Order by name.
problems.solution: SELECT e.emp_name FROM emp e WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp WHERE dept_id = e.dept_id) ORDER BY e.emp_name;
problems.hint: The inner query refers to the outer row (`e.dept_id`) — a correlated subquery.

problems.title: Customers with no orders
problems.statement: Show the `name` of customers who have **never placed an order**.
problems.solution: SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);

problems.title: Rank within department
problems.statement: For employees with a department show `dept_id`, `emp_name`, `salary` and `rnk`: the salary rank **within the department** (highest = 1, ties share a rank). Order by `dept_id`, `rnk`, `emp_name`.
problems.solution: SELECT dept_id, emp_name, salary, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk FROM emp WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY dept_id, rnk, emp_name;
problems.hint: `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)`.

problems.title: Second highest per department
problems.statement: Table `staff(id, dept_id, salary, hire_date)` has ties. For each department return every row whose salary is the **second highest distinct** salary of that department: `dept_id`, `id`, `salary`. Order by `dept_id`, `id`.
problems.solution: SELECT dept_id, id, salary FROM (SELECT dept_id, id, salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk FROM staff) WHERE rnk = 2 ORDER BY dept_id, id;
problems.hint: `DENSE_RANK` (no gaps after ties). A window function cannot be used in `WHERE`, so use a subquery.

problems.title: Running total
problems.statement: For `monthly_sales(month, amount)` show `month`, `amount` and `running_total`, ordered by month.
problems.solution: SELECT month, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS running_total FROM monthly_sales ORDER BY month;
problems.hint: A window with `ORDER BY` accumulates. Add an explicit frame.

problems.title: Month-over-month change
problems.statement: Show `month`, `amount` and `prev_amount` (the previous month's amount, NULL for the first month), ordered by month.
problems.solution: SELECT month, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_amount FROM monthly_sales ORDER BY month;
problems.hint: `LAG(col)` looks at the previous row of the window.

problems.title: Login streaks (gaps and islands)
problems.statement: `logins(user_id, login_day)` has one row per user per day (ISO dates). Return each **streak of consecutive days**: `user_id`, `streak_start`, `streak_end`, `days`. Order by `user_id`, `streak_start`.
problems.solution: SELECT user_id, MIN(login_day) AS streak_start, MAX(login_day) AS streak_end, COUNT(*) AS days FROM (SELECT user_id, login_day, date(login_day, '-' || ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_day) || ' day') AS grp FROM logins) GROUP BY user_id, grp ORDER BY user_id, streak_start;
problems.oracle:
SELECT user_id, MIN(login_day) AS streak_start, MAX(login_day) AS streak_end, COUNT(*) AS days
FROM (SELECT user_id, login_day,
             login_day - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_day) AS grp
      FROM logins)
GROUP BY user_id, grp
ORDER BY user_id, streak_start;
problems.hint: Number each user's days with `ROW_NUMBER()` and subtract that number from the date. Within a streak the result is constant — group by it.
problems.explain: In an unbroken run the date and the row number both grow by 1, so `date - row_number` stays constant; any gap changes it. Group by that constant.

problems.title: Missing ticket numbers
problems.statement: `tickets(ticket_no, ...)` should be 1..10 but has gaps. Show each gap as `gap_from`, `gap_to`, ordered by `gap_from`.
problems.solution: SELECT ticket_no + 1 AS gap_from, next_no - 1 AS gap_to FROM (SELECT ticket_no, LEAD(ticket_no) OVER (ORDER BY ticket_no) AS next_no FROM tickets) WHERE next_no - ticket_no > 1 ORDER BY gap_from;
problems.hint: Compare each number with the next one (`LEAD`).

problems.title: Find duplicate emails
problems.statement: List the emails that appear **more than once** in `contacts`, with how many times (`times`). Order by email.
problems.solution: SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS times FROM contacts GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY email;

problems.title: Delete duplicates, keep one
problems.statement: Delete the duplicate rows in `contacts`, keeping the row with the **smallest id** for each email. Finish with a `SELECT * FROM contacts ORDER BY id;` (the last result set is what gets checked).
problems.solution:
DELETE FROM contacts WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT MIN(id) FROM contacts GROUP BY email);
SELECT * FROM contacts ORDER BY id;
problems.hint: Which id do you want to keep in each group?

problems.title: Pivot quarters into columns
problems.statement: From `qsales(product, quarter, amount)` produce one row per product with columns `q1`, `q2`, `q3`, `q4` (NULL if no sales) and `total`. Order by product.
problems.solution: SELECT product, SUM(CASE WHEN quarter='Q1' THEN amount END) AS q1, SUM(CASE WHEN quarter='Q2' THEN amount END) AS q2, SUM(CASE WHEN quarter='Q3' THEN amount END) AS q3, SUM(CASE WHEN quarter='Q4' THEN amount END) AS q4, SUM(amount) AS total FROM qsales GROUP BY product ORDER BY product;
problems.hint: `SUM(CASE WHEN quarter = 'Q1' THEN amount END)` per output column.

problems.title: Customers who bought every product
problems.statement: Tables `products` and `purchases(customer, product_id)`. List the customers who bought **every** product (a customer may buy the same product twice). Order by customer.
problems.solution: SELECT customer FROM purchases GROUP BY customer HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products) ORDER BY customer;
problems.hint: Compare the customer's number of *distinct* products with the total number of products.

problems.title: Swap two values with one UPDATE
problems.statement: In `members`, `F` and `M` were entered the wrong way round. Fix it with a **single UPDATE**, then finish with `SELECT * FROM members ORDER BY id;`.
problems.solution:
UPDATE members SET gender = CASE gender WHEN 'F' THEN 'M' WHEN 'M' THEN 'F' END;
SELECT * FROM members ORDER BY id;
problems.hint: Two separate updates would turn everyone into the same value. A single UPDATE with CASE evaluates every row against the *old* values.

problems.title: Org chart with levels
problems.statement: Using the manager relationship in `emp`, list every employee with their `level` (the CEO = 1, the CEO's reports = 2, ...). Show `emp_name`, `level`. Order by `level`, then `emp_name`.
problems.solution: WITH RECURSIVE org(emp_id, emp_name, lvl) AS (SELECT emp_id, emp_name, 1 FROM emp WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.emp_id, e.emp_name, o.lvl + 1 FROM emp e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.emp_id) SELECT emp_name, lvl AS level FROM org ORDER BY lvl, emp_name;
problems.oracle:
SELECT emp_name, LEVEL AS lvl
FROM emp
START WITH manager_id IS NULL
CONNECT BY PRIOR emp_id = manager_id
ORDER BY LEVEL, emp_name;
problems.hint: Anchor member: the employee with no manager. Recursive member: employees whose manager is in the previous round.

problems.title: Hires per year
problems.statement: Show the number of employees hired in each year: `yr` and `hired`, for years 2020 and later, ordered by year. (`hire_date` is an ISO date string.)
problems.solution: SELECT CAST(strftime('%Y', hire_date) AS INTEGER) AS yr, COUNT(*) AS hired FROM emp WHERE hire_date >= '2020-01-01' GROUP BY yr ORDER BY yr;
problems.oracle:
SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date) AS yr, COUNT(*) AS hired
FROM emp
WHERE hire_date >= DATE '2020-01-01'
GROUP BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date)
ORDER BY yr;
problems.note: SQLite has no `EXTRACT`; it uses `strftime('%Y', date)`. Oracle uses `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM date)`.

problems.title: String functions
problems.statement: Show `emp_name` in upper case (`shout`) and its length (`len`) for employees whose name has **exactly 5 letters**. Order by name.
problems.solution: SELECT UPPER(emp_name) AS shout, LENGTH(emp_name) AS len FROM emp WHERE LENGTH(emp_name) = 5 ORDER BY emp_name;
